hints: Start by reminding yourself which kingdoms these two organisms belong to - a fungus and a flowering plant - and what basic cell features separate those kingdoms.
Now link structure to way of life: think about cell wall material and chloroplasts, then about how each organism gains its organic food - from a host or by making it.
walkthrough:
Sort Out Structure - Fungus Versus Plant**
You are comparing a fungus with a maize plant. Fungi do not have chloroplasts and their walls are made of chitin, not cellulose. Their body is a mycelium of long branching hyphae, often with several nuclei per compartment. Plants have cellulose walls, chloroplasts for photosynthesis, and organised tissues, not hyphae.

Link To Function - Feeding**
Because it lacks chloroplasts, E. turcicum cannot photosynthesise. It is a heterotroph and here a parasite, absorbing digested food from the maize leaves it damages. Z. mays is an autotroph, or phototroph, that photosynthesises to make its own organic compounds. Give one clear paired contrast for structure and one for function.

Final answer: Structural: E. turcicum has chitin cell walls / no chloroplasts / hyphae of long branching multinucleate cells; Z. mays has cellulose cell walls / chloroplasts / no hyphae. Functional: E. turcicum is heterotrophic / parasitic and obtains food from host, no photosynthesis; Z. mays is autotrophic / photosynthetic.

hints: Think about the shape of classification - do we start with a few very large groups or many very small groups, and what happens at each lower level?
Ask yourself what puts organisms in the same group - is it differences or common shared features like anatomy, DNA and phylogeny?
Recall the order of the main ranks from large to small and what the last two ranks together give you.
Apply this to the two named species - what very large group do they share as eukaryotes, and at which level do they first separate?
walkthrough:
The Hierarchy Idea**
Classification is nested. You start with large groups containing many organisms with only a few features in common, then divide into smaller and smaller groups. Members of a smaller group share more features in common.

The Ranks In Order**
Learn the sequence: kingdom - phylum - class - order - family - genus - species. You need three of kingdom to family for credit. The final two, genus and species, together form the binomial, Latin scientific name, such as Exserohilum turcicum and Zea mays.

Place These Two Organisms**
Both are eukaryotes, so both are in domain Eukarya. They diverge at kingdom level into Fungi and Plantae. That shows how hierarchy reflects evolutionary relatedness - shared at the top, different lower down.

Final answer: Organisms are placed in a hierarchy of successively smaller groups with shared features; sequence kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species; genus + species gives binomial scientific name; both in domain Eukarya but different kingdoms Fungi and Plantae.

hints: Think about what the x-axis measures - if a plant has a small percentage area of damage, has the fungus succeeded or failed?
Now read the two arrow positions for the parents on the x-axis and decide which lower value means greater resistance.
walkthrough:
Interpret Damage As Resistance**
The x-axis is percentage area of leaf damage. More damage means less defence. So low damage equals high resistance to infection by E. turcicum.

Read The Parental Means**
The arrows mark the parental means. SKV50 is at about 22% damage on the left, CML153 is at about 58% damage on the right. Because SKV50 has the much lower mean damage, it is the more resistant parent variety.
Final answer: Low % leaf damage indicates high resistance; mean for SKV50 is approx 22% and for CML153 is approx 58%, so SKV50 shows greater resistance.

hints: Look at the shape in Fig. 2.1 - bars for every intermediate value forming a smooth normal curve with no distinct classes - which type of variation does that show?
walkthrough:
Spot The Normal Distribution**
The F2 histogram shows a full range of intermediate phenotypes from about 20% to 60% damage with a bell-shaped normal curve. There are no discrete categories. That is the hallmark of continuous variation.

hints: Recall what kind of genetic control produces a smooth normal curve rather than 3:1 ratios - one gene or many genes?
Think about whether all those genes affect different traits or the same quantitative trait like percentage damage.
Consider how large the effect of each single allele is in this system - major on-off effect or small?
Put it together - how do the small effects of different genes combine to give the full range in the F2?
walkthrough:
Many Genes, One Trait**
Continuous variation is caused by polygenic inheritance. That means many different genes, or polygenes, all influence the same quantitative trait - here percentage area of leaf damage, or resistance.

Small And Additive Effects**
No single gene decides resistant or susceptible. Each allele contributes only a small effect, for example increasing or decreasing damage slightly. The final phenotype is the sum of all these additive, combined effects plus environment.

Why The F2 Looks Like This**
The F1 hybrids are heterozygous at many loci. When self-crossed, segregation and independent assortment reshuffle many alleles, producing F2 plants with every combination from mostly resistance alleles to mostly susceptibility alleles. That gives the normal distribution centred near 40%.

Final answer: Resistance / leaf damage is controlled by many / several genes (polygenes); all affect the same trait; each allele has a small effect; effects are additive / combined to give a range of phenotypes.
